fetched_contents.text: On the use of Raman spectroscopy to characterize mass-produced graphene nanoplatelets Abstract Raman spectroscopy is one of the most common methods to characterize graphene-related 2D materials, providing information on a wide range of physical and chemical properties. Because of typical sample inhomogeneity, Raman spectra are acquired from several locations across a sample, and analysis is carried out on the averaged spectrum from all locations. This is then used to characterize the “quality” of the graphene produced, in particular the level of exfoliation for top-down manufactured materials. However, these have generally been developed using samples prepared with careful separation of unexfoliated materials. In this work we assess these metrics when applied to non-ideal samples, where unexfoliated graphite has been deliberately added to the exfoliated material. We demonstrate that previously published metrics, when applied to averaged spectra, do not allow the presence of this unexfoliated material to be reliably detected. Furthermore, when a sufficiently large number of spectra are acquired, it is found that by processing and classifying individual spectra, rather than the averaged spectrum, it is possible to identify the presence of this material in the sample, although quantification of the amount remains approximate. We therefore recommend this approach as a robust methodology for reliable characterization of mass-produced graphene-related 2D materials using confocal Raman spectroscopy. Keywords: few-layer graphene, graphene, metrology, quality control, Raman spectroscopy Introduction Graphene and related 2D materials (GR2Ms) are now well established with commercial products available across a range of sectors, from sports and leisure products [1–2], through mobile phones [3] to automotive applications [4]. There are also a large number of producers of these materials [5], offering an array of products with a wide range of properties such as improved mechanical strength and higher thermal conductivity. To accelerate the further development and adoption of GR2Ms, it is critical to develop reliable and standardized methods to characterize the materials being produced and purchased. The publication of international standards is a key step in this process, such as recent publications on nomenclature [6] and structural characterization [7]. The measurement methods described in these standards, however, can be time-consuming and expensive. As the range of applications for GR2Ms expands, and with it the production volumes, there is an increasing need for faster methods that can be applied in-line or at-line. These quality control methods do not need the same level of accuracy and precision as those specified in international standards, but they do need to be validated against those methods. What is more important is repeatability and reproducibility, to allow for product monitoring over time. They also need to be able to provide results quickly, in a form that is easy to interpret, providing simple pass/fail outcomes. Raman spectroscopy is one of the most widely used characterization tool for GR2Ms [8]. A search of Web of Science showed that of 97,532 articles published in the last five years with “Graphene” in the abstract, 9.3% also mentioned “Raman”. This is compared with atomic force microscopy (AFM) (2.4%), scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (11.4%), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (7.2%) or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (5.6%). It has the advantages of relatively low cost, simple sample preparation, quick measurements, and automated analysis, offering clear benefits for quality control applications. It has been demonstrated in several application areas as an in-line process analysis and control method [9–12]. Raman spectroscopy is particularly suited to the analysis of graphitic materials because of the large scattering cross section of graphitic materials and the large amount of information obtainable from a single measurement. For example, information on flake size, extent of structural defects, chemical or electronic doping, and strain and layer number can all be extracted from one spectrum [13–18]. As such, Raman spectroscopy is widely used by producers to assess the quality of their material, in particular the absence of graphite or nanoscale graphite. It is important to recall that graphene has been defined as a “single layer of carbon atoms with each atom bound to three neighbours in a honeycomb structure” with materials with more than one layer defined as “few-layer graphene” or “graphene nanoplatelets” [6]. This assessment is generally based on examining the shape of the so-called 2D peak (ca. 2700 cm−1), which, for Bernal stacking, shows clear changes on going from single-layer through few-layer graphene to graphite [19]. Bulk graphite typically shows a signal comprising two components, sometimes referred to as 2D1 and 2D2, with intensities approximately one fourth and half of that of the so-called G peak (ca. 1580 cm−1) [20]. In contrast, single-layer graphene typically yields a 2D peak comprising a single component, with an intensity of around double that of the G peak [19]. In between these two extremes, the peak shape evolves gradually, and while the 2D peak from bilayer graphene has been shown to comprise four components, deconvolution for higher layer numbers has not been reliably carried out. The spectrum recorded from flakes with ten or more layers is typically indistinguishable from that of bulk graphite. However, it is important to note that this behaviour can be affected by the stacking order. For example, for turbostratic graphite, where there is random rotational alignment between the layers, the 2D band also has the shape of a single Lorentzian line [21]. Abstract To attain the expected outcomes of any measurement, probing the quality of graphene is a prerequisite among the various graphene samples. Herein, we investigate the identification of the number of layers in mechanically exfoliated graphene using Raman spectroscopy. The intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width of the 2D peak have been used to distinguish the number of layers. The 2D peak consists of a single Lorentzian fit having peak width 24 cm−1 in single layer graphene (SLG) and splits into four, six and five components for bilayer, trilayer, and five layers respectively. Further, the quality of graphene has been analyzed by I2D/IG, Raman mapping and the charge carrier mobility. In addition, the high quality of graphene has been encapsulated in terms of two phonon scattering processes and the variation in I2D/IG of SLG as a result of crossover from electron-electron to electron-hole scattering. The maximum mobility of SLG has been obtained ∼11,931 cm2V−1s−1 when the peak width and I2D/IG are 23.88 cm−1 and 5.36 respectively. Hence, the present study sets a platform to use Raman scattering as a probe for quantification of graphene layers and Raman mapping with spatial resolution provides the solution for specific area selection to fabricate the next generation graphene based quantum devices. This first two-dimensional material renders a platform to study the quantum electrodynamics in the experimental condensed matter physics [3,4]. A multitudinous phenomena have been observed such as half-integer Quantum Hall Effect (QHE) in SLG where Hall plateaus are in terms of 4e2hN+12 and conventional QHE in bilayer graphene in terms of 4e2hN, where N is an integer, apart from these the existence of non-zero Berry’s phase in bilayer graphene, and appearance of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene and trilayer graphene superlattice, etc. in last 1.5 decades [[4], [5], [6], [7], [8]]. The manipulation of electron transport is the requirement of present-day electronics [9,10]. Graphene unique properties from mechanical to electronic are very sensitive to the thickness and make it a propitious candidate to study the fundamental physics and the realization of the various potential applications [[11], [12], [13]]. The above-mentioned observations clearly indicate that layer number identification becomes essential and there are certain metric parameters such as Fermi level, edge structure, defects, thermal conductivity and number of layers to distinguish the graphene layers [14]. Measurement of any one of these parameters can be treated as the metrological technique. Raman Spectroscopy is one of the non-ruinous, non-ambiguous and fast technique to characterize the graphene samples [15]. The non-existence of bandgap and the unique nature of the π-electron dispersion in graphene makes all incident wavelength resonant. Abstract Graphene-based materials, including composites with metals, metal oxides, or polymers, demonstrate enhanced vibrational, electronic, and mechanical properties, rendering them highly promising for applications in energy, sensing, and catalysis. Vibrational spectroscopy is extensively used to characterize these materials, with primary focus on the G band (first-order in-plane vibrational band), the 2D band (second-order overtone), and the defect-activated D band. Although the D band frequently appears in chemically modified or structurally complex graphene systems, its spectral characteristics, such as peak position, linewidth, and relative intensity, alongside variations in the G and 2D bands, are often underreported or inadequately interpreted. This review underscores the critical importance of the D band in assessing disorder, edge structure, doping, and matrix interactions within graphene-based materials. Introduction Graphene-based composites, a class of hybrid materials that integrate graphene with metals, metal oxides, polymers, or other functional components, have received significant attention over the past few decades for their ability to enhance the performance of electrochemical devices, including supercapacitors, electrocatalysts, sensors, and fuel cells [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Among the most effective strategies for tailoring graphene’s electronic characteristics is chemical doping, typically introduced during the synthesis of such composites through the incorporation of heteroatoms into the graphene lattice or onto its surface [12]. Doping in graphene can be broadly classified into p-type and n-type, depending on the electronic nature of the dopant, and is commonly achieved through chemical or electrical methods [12], [14], [15], [16], [17], with chemical routes dominating in composite fabrication. Two principal doping mechanisms are generally recognized: surface transfer doping and substitutional doping [12]. Methods to assess quality and defect density using Raman spectroscopy

Raman spectroscopy assesses graphene-related quality and defect density through several interrelated metrics, with the D peak and 2D peak being central. The D band’s intensity is widely used as a defect-density indicator: the I(D)/I(G) ratio is a commonly used metric to evaluate defect density in graphene-based materials, and studies emphasize that the D band’s peak position, linewidth, and intensity are often underreported or insufficiently interpreted [N3-F3]. In addition, the D peak’s relative intensity can be affected by laser excitation energy, which means that I(D)/I(G) is not always a universal metric and depends on the excitation conditions [N3-R2]. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the D peak also matters, because broader D peaks can indicate more disorder or more complex defect states [N3-F3].

The 2D peak shape is another key quality indicator. The 2D peak is used to distinguish layer number and estimate quality, with its intensity and width providing valuable information about defects, doping, strain, and interfacial effects [N3-F3]. In graphene-related materials, the 2D peak shape evolves with increasing layer number: single-layer graphene typically yields a sharp single-component 2D peak, while few-layer graphene and bulk graphite show broader, more complex shapes [N1-F1]. This means that disorder can be assessed not only by the absolute D intensity but also by how the 2D peak broadens or changes shape. A broader 2D peak is often associated with more disorder or more layers, and the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe the number of layers and quality [N2-F2]. The 2D peak is also sensitive to stacking order and strain; for example, turbostratic graphite typically has a single Lorentzian 2D band but with a much larger width than single-layer graphene [N1-F1]. These observations show that 2D peak shape and disorder are tightly linked: disorder can broaden peaks, shift their positions, and change their relative intensities, making shape analysis a necessary part of quality assessment [N3-F3].

Common quantitative Raman metrics for quality evaluation include I(D)/I(G), I(2D)/I(G), and the 2D peak width. The review explicitly states that I(D)/I(G) is used to quantify defect density and that I(2D)/I(G) is commonly used to assess layer number [N3-F3]. The same source also emphasizes that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. Another source states that the intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width of the 2D peak are used to distinguish the number of layers and probe quality [N2-F2]. It also notes that the I2D/IG ratio is important for identifying the number of layers and that the variation in this ratio can be qualitatively described in terms of first- and second-order scattering processes [N2-F2]. Thus, the standard quality metrics are not limited to just one ratio; they combine intensity ratios with peak width and shape analysis.

Sample preparation and laser excitation conditions strongly influence defect quantification. The evidence shows that the I(D)/I(G) ratio can depend on laser excitation energy [N3-R2], and that laser wavelength and polarization can affect Raman measurements [N5-R2]. The Raman spectroscopy overview also emphasizes that sample preparation and quick measurements are advantages of the technique, but it also implies that the observed spectra depend on how the material is prepared [N4-F4]. In particular, the Raman signal can be affected by the optical cavity formed by the sample and the substrate, and the material’s sensitivity to electric, magnetic, band structure, and temperature changes means that preparation can alter the apparent spectral features [N4-F4]. Additionally, the evidence on graphene nanoplatelets notes that sample inhomogeneity requires spectra to be acquired from multiple locations and averaged, which can obscure small amounts of unexfoliated material [N1-F1]. This means that defect quantification is not purely intrinsic to the material; it is also shaped by how the sample is collected, averaged, and excited.

Overall, Raman quality assessment combines I(D)/I(G) as a defect-density metric, I(2D)/I(G) and 2D peak width as layer-number and disorder indicators, and peak shape analysis as a way to detect structural perturbations and stacking effects [N3-F3][N2-F2]. However, laser excitation energy and sample preparation can change the observed values, so defect quantification must be interpreted with caution [N3-R2][N5-R2]. The evidence supports a broad conclusion: quality is assessed through a combination of peak intensity, peak shape, and excitation-dependent response, rather than a single absolute metric [N3-F3][N2-F2].

Scientific basis for differentiating graphene from graphene nanoplatelets

The scientific basis for distinguishing graphene from graphene nanoplatelets in Raman spectroscopy relies on the 2D/G intensity ratio, peak shape, and the effects of layer thickness, stacking, and particle morphology. In single-layer graphene (SLG), the 2D peak is sharp and typically much stronger than the G peak, with a single-component shape [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In contrast, bulk graphite typically shows two components in the 2D band, with intensities roughly one fourth and half of the G peak [N1-F1]. For few-layer graphene, the 2D peak broadens and its shape changes gradually, while turbostratic graphite also has a single Lorentzian 2D band but with a much larger width [N1-F1]. These differences suggest that the 2D/G intensity ratio is not sufficient on its own to distinguish between graphene and graphene nanoplatelets; the peak shape and broader 2D behavior are equally important [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Layer thickness and stacking order strongly affect the Raman spectrum. The evidence explicitly says that the intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width of the 2D peak are used to distinguish the number of layers [N2-F2]. It also states that the 2D peak shape evolves gradually with increasing layer number and that the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe quality [N3-F3]. In addition, the overview notes that the Raman spectrum of strained graphene, doped graphene, and defected graphene changes as a function of these structural features, making the 2D peak a sensitive probe of layer number and disorder [N4-F4]. This means that graphene nanoplatelets, which are generally defined as few-layer graphene or multilayer graphene rather than a single layer [N1-F1], will typically show broader, more complex 2D bands compared with SLG. The same source also emphasizes that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3].

Particle morphology and sample inhomogeneity can affect identification. The graphene nanoplatelet literature notes that Raman spectra are acquired from several locations across a sample, and analysis is usually carried out on the averaged spectrum [N1-F1]. This is because typical samples are inhomogeneous, and the averaged spectrum is used to characterize the “quality” of the material. However, the same work also shows that previously published metrics can fail to detect unexfoliated material when applied to averaged spectra, and that processing individual spectra can reveal the presence of unexfoliated material even when quantification remains approximate [N1-F1]. This matters because graphene nanoplatelets are often not perfectly homogeneous, and their morphology may include aggregated or defective regions. The evidence also says that Raman spectroscopy is sensitive to any changes in electric or magnetic fields, band structure, and temperature, and that it is especially useful for layered materials [N4-F4]. So, even when the sample appears to be few-layer graphene, aggregation or defective regions can change the observed spectrum and make it harder to assign a precise layer count [N1-F1][N4-F4].

The review on graphene-based materials also highlights that the D band is important for assessing disorder, edge structure, doping, and matrix interactions, and that its spectral characteristics are often underreported or inadequately interpreted [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that the presence of aggregated or defective regions can distort the identification of graphene versus graphene nanoplatelets: defects can increase the D intensity, broaden D and G peaks, and alter the 2D peak shape [N3-F3]. The evidence also states that the intensity ratio I(D)/I(G), peak positions, and full width at half maximum of the D, G, and 2D bands are particularly sensitive to defects and dopant interactions [N3-F3]. Therefore, the identification of graphene versus graphene nanoplatelets depends not only on the 2D/G ratio but also on the full shape of the peaks, the presence of D-band features, and the stacking/layering context.

Regarding interlayer coupling or splitting effects, the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. The overview on graphene and related materials states that the band structure of SLG and multilayer graphene is reflected in the shape of the 2D peak [N4-F4]. It also notes that the 2D peak splits into multiple components as layer number increases, with bilayer graphene showing four, trilayer five, and five-layer six components [N2-F2]. The Raman spectroscopy of graphene and related materials overview explicitly states that the shape of the 2D peak is sensitive to stacking order and strain [N4-F4]. A separate source on graphene nanoplatelets production notes that the 2D-protocol is based on the parameterized principal component analysis of the two-phonon 2D band and measures interlayer coupling [N6-R1]. This suggests that interlayer coupling is a relevant feature in graphene nanoplatelets, but the evidence does not provide a direct experimental statement that graphene nanoplatelets show interlayer splitting in the same way as bilayer graphene. Instead, the available evidence points to interlayer coupling and stacking effects as important contributors to the 2D peak shape, rather than to a simple splitting of the G band [N6-R1][N4-F4]. The broader conclusion is that graphene nanoplatelets can show interlayer coupling effects, but the provided evidence does not establish unambiguous splitting of the G band itself.

Practical considerations and limitations of Raman-based differentiation

Sample preparation has a major impact on spectral interpretation. The evidence shows that graphene-related samples are often inhomogeneous, so Raman spectra are acquired from multiple locations and averaged [N1-F1]. This is necessary because unexfoliated graphite can be present in the sample, and previously published metrics applied to averaged spectra do not reliably detect it [N1-F1]. The same source also states that processing individual spectra can identify unexfoliated material, although quantification remains approximate [N1-F1]. This indicates that sample preparation can mask true material composition or layer information, because averaging can smooth out small amounts of impurity or unexfoliated regions. The Raman spectroscopy overview further notes that sample preparation and quick measurements are advantages of the technique, but it also implies that the spectral response depends on how the material is prepared [N4-F4]. In particular, the optical cavity formed by the sample and substrate can influence the observed spectrum, and the material’s sensitivity to electric, magnetic, band structure, and temperature changes means that preparation can alter the apparent Raman features [N4-F4].

Excitation wavelength and polarization dependence are also important. The evidence says that laser excitation at 633 nm is commonly used, and that excitation energy can affect the I(D)/I(G) ratio [N5-R1][N3-R2]. It also notes that polarized Raman is a promising technique because the lasers used are naturally linearly polarized, and polarized microscopic laser Raman scattering spectroscopy has been used to systematically analyze edge details [N5-R2][N5-R3]. This means that polarization can reveal anisotropic features, such as edge structure or stacking effects, and that excitation wavelength can change the observed intensity ratios and peak positions [N5-R2][N3-R2]. The evidence also mentions polarization dependence of Raman peaks in twisted bilayer graphene, showing that polarization can be used to probe structure [N5-R4]. However, the same evidence does not provide a direct statement that all Raman features are equally sensitive to polarization; rather, it shows that polarization can be a useful tool in certain contexts [N5-R2][N5-R4].

Limitations in distinguishing similar materials or low-quality samples are considerable. The review on graphene-based materials emphasizes that the D band is important for assessing disorder, edge structure, doping, and matrix interactions, but that its spectral characteristics are often underreported or inadequately interpreted [N3-F3]. This suggests that Raman can easily be misinterpreted when disorder is high or when the sample is defective. The graphene nanoplatelet study further shows that averaged spectra can obscure unexfoliated material, and that metrics applied to averaged spectra may not detect it reliably [N1-F1]. The overview on graphene and related materials notes that the Raman spectrum of defected graphene is sensitive to defects, and that the intensity ratio I(D)/I(G), peak positions, and FWHM are particularly sensitive to defects and dopant interactions [N3-F3]. These points imply that low-quality samples, defective regions, or samples with mixed phases are especially hard to distinguish using Raman alone, because the same spectral features can arise from different causes [N3-F3][N1-F1].

Nanoplatelet morphology can mask true layer information. The evidence states that graphene nanoplatelets are typically characterized by acquiring spectra from multiple locations and averaging them [N1-F1], because the samples are inhomogeneous. It also notes that unexfoliated graphite can be present in the sample and that averaged spectra may not reliably detect it [N1-F1]. This means that the observed spectrum can reflect morphology rather than true layer count: aggregates or defective regions may dominate the signal, while true few-layer graphene may be underrepresented or hidden [N1-F1]. The overview on graphene and related materials further notes that the 2D peak shape is sensitive to stacking order and strain [N4-F4], which implies that particle morphology and stacking can change the apparent layer count. The evidence also shows that the intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width are used to distinguish the number of layers, but that these metrics can be affected by laser excitation energy and by sample preparation [N2-F2][N3-R2]. Taken together, these limitations indicate that Raman-based differentiation is not foolproof: the same material can look different depending on sample preparation, excitation conditions, and morphology, and low-quality or aggregated samples can be particularly difficult to interpret [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R2].

Methods to assess quality and defect density using Raman spectroscopy

Raman spectroscopy assesses graphene-related quality and defect density through several interrelated metrics, with the D peak and 2D peak being central. The D band’s intensity is widely used as a defect-density indicator: the I(D)/I(G) ratio is a commonly used metric to evaluate defect density in graphene-based materials, and studies emphasize that the D band’s peak position, linewidth, and intensity are often underreported or insufficiently interpreted [N3-F3]. In addition, the D peak’s relative intensity can be affected by laser excitation energy, which means that I(D)/I(G) is not always a universal metric and depends on the excitation conditions [N3-R2]. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the D peak also matters, because broader D peaks can indicate more disorder or more complex defect states [N3-F3].

The 2D peak shape is another key quality indicator. The 2D peak is used to distinguish layer number and estimate quality, with its intensity and width providing valuable information about defects, doping, strain, and interfacial effects [N3-F3]. In graphene-related materials, the 2D peak shape evolves with increasing layer number: single-layer graphene typically yields a sharp single-component 2D peak, while few-layer graphene and bulk graphite show broader, more complex shapes [N1-F1]. This means that disorder can be assessed not only by the absolute D intensity but also by how the 2D peak broadens or changes shape. A broader 2D peak is often associated with more disorder or more layers, and the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe the number of layers and quality [N2-F2]. The 2D peak is also sensitive to stacking order and strain; for example, turbostratic graphite typically has a single Lorentzian 2D band but with a much larger width than single-layer graphene [N1-F1]. These observations show that 2D peak shape and disorder are tightly linked: disorder can broaden peaks, shift their positions, and change their relative intensities, making shape analysis a necessary part of quality assessment [N3-F3].

Common quantitative Raman metrics for quality evaluation include I(D)/I(G), I(2D)/I(G), and the 2D peak width. The review explicitly states that I(D)/I(G) is used to quantify defect density and that I(2D)/I(G) is commonly used to assess layer number [N3-F3]. The same source also emphasizes that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. Another source states that the intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width of the 2D peak are used to distinguish the number of layers and probe quality [N2-F2]. It also notes that the I2D/IG ratio is important for identifying the number of layers and that the variation in this ratio can be qualitatively described in terms of first- and second-order scattering processes [N2-F2]. Thus, the standard quality metrics are not limited to just one ratio; they combine intensity ratios with peak width and shape analysis.

Sample preparation and laser excitation conditions strongly influence defect quantification. These differences suggest that the 2D/G intensity ratio is not sufficient on its own to distinguish between graphene and graphene nanoplatelets; the peak shape and broader 2D behavior are equally important [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Layer thickness and stacking order strongly affect the Raman spectrum. The evidence explicitly says that the intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width of the 2D peak are used to distinguish the number of layers [N2-F2]. It also states that the 2D peak shape evolves gradually with increasing layer number and that the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe quality [N3-F3]. In addition, the overview notes that the Raman spectrum of strained graphene, doped graphene, and defected graphene changes as a function of these structural features, making the 2D peak a sensitive probe of layer number and disorder [N4-F4]. This means that graphene nanoplatelets, which are generally defined as few-layer graphene or multilayer graphene rather than a single layer [N1-F1], will typically show broader, more complex 2D bands compared with SLG. The same source also emphasizes that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3].

Particle morphology and sample inhomogeneity can affect identification. The graphene nanoplatelet literature notes that Raman spectra are acquired from several locations across a sample, and analysis is usually carried out on the averaged spectrum [N1-F1]. This is because typical samples are inhomogeneous, and the averaged spectrum is used to characterize the “quality” of the material. However, the same work also shows that previously published metrics can fail to detect unexfoliated material when applied to averaged spectra, and that processing individual spectra can reveal the presence of unexfoliated material even when quantification remains approximate [N1-F1]. ## How Raman spectroscopy differentiates graphene from graphene nanoplatelets and assesses their quality

Raman spectroscopy differentiates graphene from graphene nanoplatelets by analyzing the **2D/G intensity ratio**, **2D peak shape**, and the broader structural and defect-related features of the spectrum. It is also used to assess quality and defect density through metrics such as **I(D)/I(G)**, **I(2D)/I(G)**, and the **2D peak width**, all of which are sensitive to layer number, stacking, disorder, and excitation conditions. The evidence shows that Raman spectroscopy is especially powerful because it is non-destructive, can extract multiple structural features from a single measurement, and is sensitive to changes in electric, magnetic, band structure, and temperature, making it ideal for layered materials such as graphene and graphene nanoplatelets [N4-F4].

## 1) How Raman spectroscopy differentiates graphene from graphene nanoplatelets

The key difference between graphene and graphene nanoplatelets lies in layer thickness, stacking, and morphology. Single-layer graphene (SLG) typically shows a **sharp, single-component 2D peak** with a much stronger intensity relative to the G peak [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In contrast, bulk graphite and few-layer graphene show broader, more complex 2D bands, with turbostratic graphite having a single Lorentzian 2D band but with a much larger width than SLG [N1-F1]. This means that the **2D/G intensity ratio alone is not sufficient** to distinguish between graphene and graphene nanoplatelets; the **peak shape** must also be considered [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 2D/G intensity ratio and peak shape
The 2D/G intensity ratio is used to estimate layer number and probe quality, while the peak shape is used to infer disorder, stacking order, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. In SLG, the 2D peak is sharp and strong, whereas in few-layer graphene and graphite, the peak broadens and changes shape [N1-F1]. The review explicitly states that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that graphene nanoplatelets, which are typically defined as few-layer graphene rather than a single layer [N1-F1], will generally show broader, more complex 2D bands compared with SLG.

### Role of layer thickness and stacking
Layer thickness and stacking order strongly affect the Raman spectrum. The evidence shows that the intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width of the 2D peak are used to distinguish the number of layers, and that the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe quality [N2-F2]. The overview also notes that the 2D peak shape evolves gradually with increasing layer number, and that the 2D peak is sensitive to stacking order and strain [N4-F4]. This means that graphene nanoplatelets, which are inherently layered, will typically exhibit different 2D peak shapes compared with single-layer graphene, and that stacking effects can further alter the observed spectrum [N2-F2][N4-F4].

### Role of particle morphology
Particle morphology and sample inhomogeneity can significantly affect identification. The graphene nanoplatelet literature notes that Raman spectra are acquired from multiple locations across a sample and analyzed using the averaged spectrum [N1-F1]. This is because typical samples are inhomogeneous, and the averaged spectrum is used to characterize the “quality” of the material. However, the same work shows that previously published metrics can fail to detect unexfoliated material when applied to averaged spectra, and that processing individual spectra can reveal the presence of unexfoliated material even when quantification remains approximate [N1-F1]. This is important because graphene nanoplatelets are often not perfectly homogeneous, and their morphology may include aggregated or defective regions. The overview on graphene and related materials also emphasizes that the Raman spectrum is sensitive to changes in electric, magnetic, band structure, and temperature, and that it is especially useful for layered materials [N4-F4]. So, even when the sample appears to be few-layer graphene, aggregation or defective regions can change the observed spectrum and make it harder to assign a precise layer count [N1-F1][N4-F4].

### Interlayer coupling or splitting effects
The evidence suggests that graphene nanoplatelets can show **interlayer coupling effects**, but it does not establish a definitive statement that graphene nanoplatelets show interlayer splitting of the G band itself. The overview on graphene and related materials states that the band structure of SLG and multilayer graphene is reflected in the shape of the 2D peak [N4-F4]. The broader conclusion is that graphene nanoplatelets can show interlayer coupling effects, but the provided evidence does not support a simple G-band splitting interpretation.

## 2) How Raman spectroscopy assesses quality and defect density

Raman spectroscopy assesses quality and defect density through several interrelated metrics. The most commonly used metrics are:

- **I(D)/I(G)**: This is a commonly used metric to evaluate defect density in graphene-based materials [N3-F3]. It is also emphasized that the D band’s peak position, linewidth, and intensity are often underreported or insufficiently interpreted [N3-F3].
- **I(2D)/I(G)**: This is commonly used to assess layer number [N3-F3].
- **2D peak width**: The peak width is used to distinguish the number of layers and probe quality [N2-F2].
- **D peak width and D peak intensity**: Broader D peaks can indicate more disorder or more complex defect states [N3-F3].

### D-peak intensity and full-width-at-half-maximum
The D peak’s intensity is directly tied to defect density, while its full width at half maximum (FWHM) reflects the degree of disorder or defect-related broadening. The review states that the intensity ratio I(D)/I(G) is used to quantify defect density, and that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. In addition, the evidence shows that the I(D)/I(G) ratio can depend on laser excitation energy [N3-R2], so defect quantification must be interpreted with caution.

### 2D peak shape and disorder
The 2D peak shape is a critical quality indicator because it reflects layer number, stacking order, strain, and disorder. The overview notes that the Raman spectrum of strained graphene, doped graphene, and defected graphene changes as a function of these structural features, making the 2D peak a sensitive probe of layer number and disorder [N4-F4]. The same source also states that the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe quality [N3-F3]. This means that disorder can broaden the 2D peak, shift its position, and change its relative intensity, making shape analysis an essential part of quality assessment [N3-F3][N4-F4].

### Common quantitative Raman metrics for quality evaluation
Common quantitative metrics include:
- **I(D)/I(G)**: for defect density [N3-F3]
- **I(2D)/I(G)**: for layer number [N3-F3]
- **2D peak width**: for layer number and quality [N2-F2]
- **Peak positions and linewidths**: for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]

These metrics are not standalone; they are used together because each provides a different kind of information. The evidence also emphasizes that the intensity ratio I(D)/I(G), peak positions, and full width at half maximum of the D, G, and 2D bands are particularly sensitive to defects and dopant interactions [N3-F3].

Raman-based differentiation is powerful, but it is also subject to several practical limitations. Sample preparation can strongly affect spectral interpretation. ## 1) How Raman spectroscopy differentiates graphene from graphene nanoplatelets

The key difference between graphene and graphene nanoplatelets lies in layer thickness, stacking, and morphology. Single-layer graphene (SLG) typically shows a **sharp, single-component 2D peak** with a much stronger intensity relative to the G peak [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In contrast, bulk graphite and few-layer graphene show broader, more complex 2D bands, with turbostratic graphite having a single Lorentzian 2D band but with a much larger width than SLG [N1-F1]. This means that the **2D/G intensity ratio alone is not sufficient** to distinguish between graphene and graphene nanoplatelets; the **peak shape** must also be considered [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 2D/G intensity ratio and peak shape
The 2D/G intensity ratio is used to estimate layer number and probe quality, while the peak shape is used to infer disorder, stacking order, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. In SLG, the 2D peak is sharp and strong, whereas in few-layer graphene and graphite, the peak broadens and changes shape [N1-F1]. The review explicitly states that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that graphene nanoplatelets, which are typically defined as few-layer graphene rather than a single layer [N1-F1], will generally show broader, more complex 2D bands compared with SLG.

### Role of layer thickness and stacking
Layer thickness and stacking order strongly affect the Raman spectrum. The evidence shows that the intensity ratio (I2D/IG) and peak width of the 2D peak are used to distinguish the number of layers, and that the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe quality [N2-F2]. The overview also notes that the 2D peak shape evolves gradually with increasing layer number, and that the 2D peak is sensitive to stacking order and strain [N4-F4]. This means that graphene nanoplatelets, which are inherently layered, will typically exhibit different 2D peak shapes compared with single-layer graphene, and that stacking effects can further alter the observed spectrum [N2-F2][N4-F4].

### Role of particle morphology
Particle morphology and sample inhomogeneity can significantly affect identification. The graphene nanoplatelet literature notes that Raman spectra are acquired from multiple locations across a sample and analyzed using the averaged spectrum [N1-F1]. This is because typical samples are inhomogeneous, and the averaged spectrum is used to characterize the “quality” of the material. However, the same work shows that previously published metrics can fail to detect unexfoliated material when applied to averaged spectra, and that processing individual spectra can reveal the presence of unexfoliated material even when quantification remains approximate [N1-F1]. This is important because graphene nanoplatelets are often not perfectly homogeneous, and their morphology may include aggregated or defective regions. The overview on graphene and related materials also emphasizes that the Raman spectrum is sensitive to changes in electric, magnetic, band structure, and temperature, and that it is especially useful for layered materials [N4-F4]. So, even when the sample appears to be few-layer graphene, aggregation or defective regions can change the observed spectrum and make it harder to assign a precise layer count [N1-F1][N4-F4].

### Interlayer coupling or splitting effects
The evidence suggests that graphene nanoplatelets can show **interlayer coupling effects**, but it does not establish a definitive statement that graphene nanoplatelets show interlayer splitting of the G band itself. The overview on graphene and related materials states that the band structure of SLG and multilayer graphene is reflected in the shape of the 2D peak [N4-F4]. It also notes that the 2D peak splits into multiple components as layer number increases, with bilayer graphene showing four, trilayer five, and five-layer six components [N2-F2]. A separate source on graphene nanoplatelet production notes that the 2D-protocol is based on the parameterized principal component analysis of the two-phonon 2D band and measures interlayer coupling [N6-R1]. This suggests that interlayer coupling is a relevant feature in graphene nanoplatelets, but the available evidence does not provide direct experimental confirmation that graphene nanoplatelets show G-band splitting in the same way as bilayer graphene [N6-R1][N4-F4]. The broader conclusion is that graphene nanoplatelets can show interlayer coupling effects, but the provided evidence does not support a simple G-band splitting interpretation.

## 2) How Raman spectroscopy assesses quality and defect density

Raman spectroscopy assesses quality and defect density through several interrelated metrics. The most commonly used metrics are:

- **I(D)/I(G)**: This is a commonly used metric to evaluate defect density in graphene-based materials [N3-F3]. It is also emphasized that the D band’s peak position, linewidth, and intensity are often underreported or insufficiently interpreted [N3-F3].
- **I(2D)/I(G)**: This is commonly used to assess layer number [N3-F3].
- **2D peak width**: The peak width is used to distinguish the number of layers and probe quality [N2-F2].
- **D peak width and D peak intensity**: Broader D peaks can indicate more disorder or more complex defect states [N3-F3].

### D-peak intensity and full-width-at-half-maximum
The D peak’s intensity is directly tied to defect density, while its full width at half maximum (FWHM) reflects the degree of disorder or defect-related broadening. The review states that the intensity ratio I(D)/I(G) is used to quantify defect density, and that the peak positions, linewidths, and relative intensities of the D, G, and 2D bands are important for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]. In addition, the evidence shows that the I(D)/I(G) ratio can depend on laser excitation energy [N3-R2], so defect quantification must be interpreted with caution.

### 2D peak shape and disorder
The 2D peak shape is a critical quality indicator because it reflects layer number, stacking order, strain, and disorder. The overview notes that the Raman spectrum of strained graphene, doped graphene, and defected graphene changes as a function of these structural features, making the 2D peak a sensitive probe of layer number and disorder [N4-F4]. The same source also states that the peak width is used in conjunction with I2D/IG to probe quality [N3-F3]. This means that disorder can broaden the 2D peak, shift its position, and change its relative intensity, making shape analysis an essential part of quality assessment [N3-F3][N4-F4].

### Common quantitative Raman metrics for quality evaluation
Common quantitative metrics include:
- **I(D)/I(G)**: for defect density [N3-F3]
- **I(2D)/I(G)**: for layer number [N3-F3]
- **2D peak width**: for layer number and quality [N2-F2]
- **Peak positions and linewidths**: for assessing disorder, interfacial effects, and structural perturbations [N3-F3]

These metrics are not standalone; they are used together because each provides a different kind of information. The evidence also emphasizes that the intensity ratio I(D)/I(G), peak positions, and full width at half maximum of the D, G, and 2D bands are particularly sensitive to defects and dopant interactions [N3-F3].

## 3) Practical considerations and limitations

Raman-based differentiation is powerful, but it is also subject to several practical limitations. Sample preparation can strongly affect spectral interpretation. The evidence shows that graphene-related samples are often inhomogeneous, so Raman spectra are acquired from multiple locations and averaged [N1-F1]. This is necessary because unexfoliated graphite can be present in the sample, and previously published metrics applied to averaged spectra do not reliably detect it [N1-F1]. The same source also states that processing individual spectra can identify unexfoliated material, although quantification remains approximate [N1-F1]. This means that sample preparation can mask true material composition or layer information, because averaging can smooth out small amounts of impurity or unexfoliated regions [N1-F1].

### Excitation wavelength and polarization dependence
Excitation wavelength and polarization can change the observed results. The evidence shows that excitation energy can affect the I(D)/I(G) ratio [N3-R2], and that polarized Raman is a promising technique because the lasers used are naturally linearly polarized [N5-R2]. Polarized microscopic laser Raman scattering spectroscopy has also been used to systematically analyze edge details [N5-R3]. The evidence also mentions polarization dependence of Raman peaks in twisted bilayer graphene, showing that polarization can be used to probe structure [N5-R4]. However, the evidence does not state that all Raman features are equally sensitive to polarization; rather, it shows that polarization can be a useful tool in certain contexts [N5-R2][N5-R4].

### Limitations in distinguishing similar materials or low-quality samples
The review emphasizes that the D band is important for assessing disorder, edge structure, doping, and matrix interactions, but that its spectral characteristics are often underreported or inadequately interpreted [N3-F3]. This suggests that Raman can easily be misinterpreted when disorder is high or when the sample is defective. The graphene nanoplatelet study further shows that averaged spectra can obscure unexfoliated material, and that metrics applied to averaged spectra may not detect it reliably [N1-F1]. The overview on graphene and related materials notes that the Raman spectrum of defected graphene is sensitive to defects, and that the intensity ratio I(D)/I(G), peak positions, and FWHM are particularly sensitive to defects and dopant interactions [N3-F3]. These points imply that low-quality samples, defective regions, or samples with mixed phases are especially hard to distinguish using Raman alone, because the same spectral features can arise from different causes [N3-F3][N1-F1].

Nanoplatelet morphology can mask true layer information because the material is often not perfectly homogeneous. The evidence states that graphene nanoplatelets are typically characterized by acquiring spectra from multiple locations and averaging them [N1-F1]. It also notes that unexfoliated graphite can be present in the sample and that averaged spectra may not reliably detect it [N1-F1]. This means that the observed spectrum can reflect morphology rather than true layer count: aggregates or defective regions may dominate the signal, while true few-layer graphene may be underrepresented or hidden [N1-F1]. The overview on graphene and related materials further notes that the 2D peak shape is sensitive to stacking order and strain [N4-F4], which implies that particle morphology and stacking can change the apparent layer count [N4-F4].
